extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and other Office personnel (and patent practitioners assessing U.S. obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103)
extracted.subtask_description: USPTO MPEP guidance for examining patent claims for obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103, including the Graham factual inquiries, search guidance, rationales to support rejections, and handling applicant replies and rebuttal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining the scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must obtain a thorough understanding of the invention disclosed and claimed by reading the specification (including the claims) to understand what the applicant has invented; give the claims the 'broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.' Once the scope of the claimed invention is determined, Office personnel must determine what to search for and where to search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Phillips v. AWH and MPEP §2111; search should cover the claimed subject matter and disclosed features which might reasonably be expected to be claimed (see MPEP §904.02). Prior art may be in the field of applicant's endeavor or reasonably pertinent to the particular problem (analogous art).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertaining the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Requires interpreting the claim language and considering both the invention and the prior art as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the claimed invention and the reference(s) as complete teachings; determine the differences and explain why those differences would or would not have been obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art
rubrics_metrics.description: Any obviousness rejection should include, either explicitly or implicitly in view of the prior art applied, an indication of the level of ordinary skill. A finding as to the level of ordinary skill may be used as a partial basis for resolving obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors to consider include: (1) type of problems encountered in the art; (2) prior art solutions to those problems; (3) rapidity with which innovations are made; (4) sophistication of the technology; (5) educational level of active workers in the field. See In re GPAC and related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective evidence / secondary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence relevant to the issue of obviousness (sometimes called 'secondary considerations') must be evaluated by Office personnel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary considerations may include commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, and unexpected results. Such evidence may be in the specification, accompany the application, or be provided timely during prosecution; weight is case-by-case and presentation alone is not dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office personnel as factfinders — articulate factual findings and rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners must ensure the written record includes findings of fact concerning the state of the art and the teachings of the references applied; factual findings are the necessary underpinnings to establish obviousness and must be articulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 35 U.S.C. 132 requires applicants be notified of the reasons for rejection. Clearly set forth findings of fact and the rationale(s) to support a rejection in an Office action to allow the applicant to decide how to proceed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search scope — what to search for
rubrics_metrics.description: The search should cover the claimed subject matter and should also cover the disclosed features which might reasonably be expected to be claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a rejection need not be based on a teaching or suggestion to combine, a preferred search is directed to finding such references if they exist (see MPEP §904.02).

rubrics_metrics.name: Search where — analogous and reasonably pertinent art
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should follow general search guidelines regarding where to search; prior art can be either in the field of applicant's endeavor or be reasonably pertinent to the particular problem with which the applicant was concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR: works available in one field can prompt predictable variations in another; see MPEP §2141.01(a) for analogous art discussion and MPEP §904 for general search guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation — broadest reasonable interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of the claimed invention must be clearly determined by giving the claims the 'broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Phillips v. AWH Corp. and MPEP §2111 for guidance on claim interpretation during examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching-Suggestion-Motivation (TSM) rationale (when present)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the search and Graham factual inquiries reveal that an obviousness rejection may be made using the familiar TSM rationale, then such a rejection should be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR cautioned against rigid application but recognized TSM as a valid rationale; where present, TSM can provide a clear teaching/suggestion/motivation to combine references (see In re Bergel and related precedent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results is an exemplary rationale supporting obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflects KSR's statement that combining familiar elements according to known methods which yields predictable results is likely to be obvious; include explicit articulation why combination would have been predictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results is an exemplary rationale supporting obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a claimed change is merely the substitution of a known element with predictable results, the combination may be obvious (see United States v. Adams discussion in KSR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a known technique to improve similar devices in the same way
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of known technique to improve similar devices (methods, or products) in the same way can support an obviousness finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a person of ordinary skill would recognize that a technique used to improve one device would improve similar devices similarly, using that technique is obvious unless its application is beyond ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement to yield predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a known technique to a known device (method, or product) ready for improvement to yield predictable results is an illustrative rationale for obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR examples demonstrate that applying routine techniques to a device ripe for improvement may be obvious when results are predictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Obvious to try' — finite predictable solutions with reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Obvious to try' can support obviousness where choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions would have had a reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR recognized 'obvious to try' as a possible rationale; such reasoning is appropriate when the solutions are finite and predictable and a person of ordinary skill would expect success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known work in one field prompting predictable variations in another field
rubrics_metrics.description: Known work in one field of endeavor may prompt variations for use in either the same or a different field based on design incentives or market forces if the variations are predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR emphasizes that cross-field teachings may be analogous when predictable variations exist; examiners should consider such cross-field references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art to modify or combine references
rubrics_metrics.description: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation (TSM) in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify or combine prior art teachings can support obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if explicit TSM is absent, implicit motivations or reasons to combine (including knowledge of a person of ordinary skill) may be relied upon, but must be articulated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of common sense in obviousness analysis must be supported
rubrics_metrics.description: Common sense can be invoked (including to supply a missing limitation), but it must be supported by evidence and a reasoned explanation; where common sense supplies a limitation that goes to the heart of the invention, the reasoned basis must be searching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Arendi v. Apple and other cases: examiners may use technical expertise but must provide a reasoned underpinning and avoid conclusory statements when relying on common sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: All claim limitations must be considered in obviousness analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: All claim limitations must be considered; while the prior art reference(s) need not teach every limitation, Office personnel must explain why the differences would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'mere existence of differences between the prior art and an invention does not establish the invention's nonobviousness' (Dann v. Johnston); explicitly articulate how each limitation factors into the analysis or why it would have been obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's reply requirements under 37 CFR 1.111(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant must distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors in the Office's action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A traverse must include a reasoned statement explaining why the Office has erred; mere statements that the PTO failed to establish a prima facie case or that reliance on common knowledge is unsupported are insufficient — examiner may repeat rejection and make next action final (see MPEP §706.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant's rebuttal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all timely rebuttal evidence when reevaluating an obviousness determination; applicants may submit secondary considerations or evidence of unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of rebuttal arguments include (A) one of ordinary skill could not have combined claimed elements by known methods (technological difficulties); (B) elements in combination do not merely perform the same separate functions; (C) the results were unexpected. Follow MPEP §2145 and consider affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art available under 35 U.S.C. 102 is available under 35 U.S.C. 103
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter that is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 can be used to support a rejection under section 103; admitted prior art can be relied upon for both anticipation and obviousness determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Panduit Corp. v. Dennison and related authority; admitted prior art may be used even if it would not qualify under statutory categories otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifying level of ordinary skill not necessary in certain situations
rubrics_metrics.description: If the only facts of record pertaining to the level of skill in the art are found within the prior art of record, an invention may be held obvious without a specific finding of a particular level of skill where the prior art itself reflects an appropriate level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Chore-Time Equipment and Okajima v. Bourdeau authority — explicit level of skill sometimes unnecessary when prior art demonstrates appropriate skill level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of ascertaining level of ordinary skill to maintain objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the art is necessary to maintain objectivity in the obviousness inquiry; the examiner must ascertain what would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill at the time of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not judge obviousness from perspective of the inventor, a layman, remote-art skilled persons, or geniuses; see Ryko Mfg. Co. v. Nu-Star and related cases.
